title: Only 7% Pass This Nursing Entrance Exam
summary: Anatomy, vital signs and patient-care decisions test whether your judgement stays sharp under pressure.

landing.intro: Body systems, vital signs and patient care—can you spot what matters and make the safest call?

about.body:
This worldwide entertainment challenge explores entrance-level nursing knowledge across 40 varied questions. It covers body systems, healthcare numeracy, observation trends, infection prevention, compassionate communication and multi-clue prioritisation.

The five challenges become progressively more applied, moving from a friendly ward briefing into observations, safety, communication, pressure decisions and a final integrated handover. Questions stay at recognition and judgement level rather than teaching diagnosis or treatment.

Your final percentage reflects only the answers given in this entertainment quiz. It is a playful snapshot of the care areas that felt strongest and the topics that proved more challenging, not a judgement of clinical competence or suitability for nursing practice.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Work through each care challenge at your own pace—there is no timer or speed bonus.
Choose the single option best supported by the visible information. Correctness stays hidden until the final reveal.
Keep going as the scenarios become harder, then reveal your score and complete answer review.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This is not an accredited nursing entrance examination, clinical assessment, professional qualification or medical advice. Healthcare procedures and responsibilities vary; always follow local policy and qualified clinical guidance.

profiles.title: The Admissions Standout
profiles.copy: You combined strong foundational knowledge with calm, careful judgement across the entire admissions lab. Details, trends and patient-centred decisions stayed clear even when the cases became more demanding.

profiles.title: The Nursing Natural
profiles.copy: You showed an excellent feel for the knowledge and judgement behind safe, compassionate care. Most of the lab’s numerical, observational and communication traps did not pull you off course.

profiles.title: The Calm Candidate
profiles.copy: You handled a broad mix of body knowledge, safety decisions and patient scenarios with steady reasoning. A few finer details kept the entrance challenge interesting.

profiles.title: The Careful Problem-Solver
profiles.copy: You built a solid result by following the evidence and treating patient safety seriously. Your strongest stage shows where your clinical-learning instincts are already taking shape.

profiles.title: The Promising Applicant
profiles.copy: You solved a good share of the admissions lab and showed useful instincts across several care areas. The answer review will reveal which concepts are ready for another look.

profiles.title: The Compassionate Explorer
profiles.copy: The lab uncovered some knowledge gaps, but it also found moments of thoughtful, patient-centred judgement. Every reviewed answer is a fresh chance to strengthen the foundations behind safe care.

insights.overview: Your nursing score at a glance

details.analysisTitle: How to read your nursing score
details.analysisCopy: This 40-question result combines body knowledge, healthcare numeracy, observation trends, infection prevention, communication and calm prioritisation. Each correct answer adds 2.5 percentage points.
details.roadmapIntro: Your score is only the first signal. Continue through the report to see which entrance areas held strongest and how your judgement changed across different care scenarios.
details.positionCopy: The entertainment challenge target is 32 correct answers out of 40. Your marker shows how close this attempt came without assessing clinical competence.
details.measuredIntro: The selected questions span three broad parts of entrance-level nursing thinking without teaching diagnosis or treatment.

measuredAreas.title: Clinical foundations
measuredAreas.copy: Following basic physiology and solving simple time, rate and measurement questions.

measuredAreas.title: Observation and priorities
measuredAreas.copy: Noticing meaningful change and using several visible clues to decide what matters first.

measuredAreas.title: Safety and communication
measuredAreas.copy: Reducing infection risk while protecting privacy, dignity and understanding.

details.tipsTitle: Three ways to sharpen clinical reasoning
details.tipsIntro: These are general quiz strategies—not clinical instruction, medical advice or a professional assessment.

tips.title: Compare with the baseline
tips.copy: A new change from the earlier condition can matter more than one isolated measurement.

tips.title: Look for immediate danger
tips.copy: Airway, breathing, circulation and sudden changes in consciousness take priority over routine comfort needs.

tips.title: Choose the concrete response
tips.copy: In communication questions, prefer the option that listens, protects dignity or checks understanding.

questions.question: Which gas has blood picked up as it returns from the lungs?
A jug contains 750 mL. Another 250 mL is added. What is the total?

visual.ariaLabel: 750 millilitres plus 250 millilitres equals what total

questions.question: A pulse changes from 72 to 88 beats per minute. What does the chart show?

visual.ariaLabel: Pulse was 72 and is now 88 beats per minute

questions.question: Your hands are visibly dirty. What is the appropriate cleaning method?
answers: Wipe them on a dry towel

questions.question: A person says, “I’m worried about what happens next.” What is the best first response?
answers: Say there is nothing to worry about
Change the subject to distract them
Acknowledge the worry and ask what concerns them most
Use technical terms to sound reassuring

questions.question: Who needs attention first?
questions.context: Person A is comfortable and asks for water. Person B has suddenly become pale and is struggling to breathe.
answers: Person B, because the sudden breathing problem may be an immediate danger
Person A, because they asked first
Both can wait until the next routine check

questions.question: What is a main function of the kidneys?
How much time passes from 09:20 to 10:05?
Which body system carries rapid electrical signals?
Where are most digested nutrients absorbed into the body?
Which change in this observation note matters most?
questions.context: Earlier: breathing comfortably and speaking normally. Now: breathing faster and pausing between short phrases.
answers: The note contains two time points

questions.question: Which detail describes a new change?
questions.context: Earlier: walking steadily and feeling well. Now: dizzy on standing and noticeably pale.
answers: The person stood up at some point

questions.question: What mismatch should be clarified?

visual.ariaLabel: Handover says left arm, chart says right arm

questions.question: Which system allows pupils to respond rapidly to light?
Which measurement changed?

visual.ariaLabel: Pulse unchanged, breathing increased, temperature unchanged and alertness unchanged

questions.question: You count 9 breaths in 30 seconds. What is the rate per minute?
A task may splash body fluid towards the face. Which protection addresses that stated risk?
answers: No protection if the task is brief

questions.question: Someone asks a sensitive question in a busy public area. What should you do?
answers: Offer to continue the conversation somewhere private
Answer briefly and quietly where you are
Ask nearby people to give you some space
Give only the non-sensitive part of the answer

questions.question: What should happen after protective gloves are removed?
answers: Only clean hands if the gloves tore

questions.question: Where should a used sharp item be placed?
answers: Directly into an approved puncture-resistant sharps container

questions.question: Shared observation equipment has just been used. What is the safest next step?
answers: Put it straight back without checking
Cover it with paper and reuse it
Clean it appropriately before the next person
Only clean it at the end of the week

questions.question: A coughing person seems embarrassed. What is the best response?
answers: Tell them off in front of everyone
Discuss their symptoms loudly across the room
Offer practical respiratory-hygiene support respectfully and protect their dignity

questions.question: A person says they did not understand an explanation. What is best?
answers: Rephrase it plainly, then ask them to explain it back in their own words
Repeat the same jargon more loudly
Tell them to search online later

questions.question: A shared communication device has been handled during care. What should happen before another person uses it?
answers: Clean it appropriately according to the stated infection-control process
Only clean the screen if it looks dusty

questions.question: What is the main problem with this fluid record?
answers: The intake is automatically too high
The reported output proves the total was normal
The entire chart should be ignored

visual.ariaLabel: Fluid chart records 800 millilitres of intake; output is blank although urine was reported twice

questions.question: Which person needs attention first?
questions.context: Person A is comfortable with a routine question. Person B has new chest discomfort, looks clammy and says they feel faint.
answers: Person A, because routine questions are quick
Both should wait for the next planned round
Person B, because several new signs suggest sudden deterioration

questions.question: Which task comes first?
questions.context: A body-fluid spill is creating a slip and exposure hazard in a walkway. A storage shelf also needs routine restocking.
answers: Restock the shelf because it was planned
Secure the immediate hazard and arrange appropriate cleaning
Leave both jobs for the next shift
Walk around the spill without warning anyone

questions.question: Who needs attention first?
questions.context: Person A is comfortable with a mildly faster pulse after walking. Person B is suddenly confused, breathing rapidly and looks pale.
answers: Person B, because several new signs suggest sudden deterioration
Person A, because their pulse changed
Both can wait for routine observations

questions.question: Which change needs prompt attention?
questions.context: Person A’s observations are unchanged and they are chatting normally. Person B was alert earlier but is now drowsy, clammy and difficult to engage.
answers: Person B’s new change from alert to drowsy and clammy
The fact that both people were observed
Neither, because exact numbers are not shown

questions.question: A person says, “I’m scared about the test.” What is the best response?
answers: Everyone has tests, so try not to think about it
I can see this is worrying you. What concerns you most?
I promise the result will be fine
Use a long technical explanation immediately

questions.question: A fluid total rises from 600 mL to 900 mL. By what percentage did it increase?
A fluid record shows 1.2 L intake and 450 mL recorded output. What is the numerical difference?
Who has immediate priority?
answers: Person A, because discomfort always comes first
Both can wait for a routine check
Person B, because consciousness and breathing have suddenly changed
Choose based on who arrived first

items: PERSON A::Alert · mild stable discomfort · normal speech
PERSON B::Pale · difficult to wake · irregular breathing
visual.ariaLabel: Person A is alert with mild stable discomfort and normal speech. Person B is pale, difficult to wake and breathing irregularly.

questions.question: What is the safest conclusion?
answers: The trend is reassuring because no exact diagnosis is given
There is clear deterioration requiring prompt qualified assessment
Wait for another shift before reporting it

visual.ariaLabel: Earlier alert with normal colour and comfortable breathing. Now confused, pale and breathing faster.

questions.question: A 1.5 L record is 40% complete. How many millilitres have been recorded?
An airway blockage prevents air reaching the lungs. What downstream effect follows most directly?

items: AIRWAY BLOCKED → LESS AIR TO LUNGS → ? → LESS OXYGEN TO TISSUES
visual.ariaLabel: Airway blocked, less air to lungs, unknown, less oxygen to tissues

answers: The kidneys immediately form more urine

questions.question: A person drinks 0.75 L, then 425 mL. What total should be recorded in mL?

visual.ariaLabel: 0.75 litres plus 425 millilitres equals what total in millilitres

questions.question: Which response best addresses both stated risks?
questions.context: A task may splash body fluid towards the eyes. Shared equipment will then be used by another person.
answers: Wear ordinary clothing and skip equipment cleaning
Only wear gloves and leave the equipment for the next person
Avoid hand hygiene because eye protection was used
Use appropriate eye or face protection, then clean shared equipment appropriately

questions.question: Which response meets both communication needs?
questions.context: A person says, “I’m frightened, and I didn’t understand what was explained.”
answers: Acknowledge the fear, explain plainly and check their understanding
Tell them the information was already given
Promise that nothing bad can happen
Ask someone else to answer without the person present

questions.question: Which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs toward the heart?

visual.ariaLabel: Lungs through unknown vessels toward the heart
